topic: 128-bit Integer Multiplication and Division in x86-64
explanation: x86-64 architecture supports 128-bit arithmetic operations, enabling calculations beyond the standard 64-bit register size.  This is crucial for handling very large integers, exceeding the capacity of a single 64-bit register.  The operations use a pair of registers (%rdx and %rax) to represent the 128-bit result, improving precision for applications requiring high-range arithmetic.
syntax: The general form of 128-bit multiplication involves using the `mulq` (unsigned) or `imulq` (signed) instructions.  The lower 64 bits of the product are stored in %rax, and the upper 64 bits in %rdx. For division, `divq` (unsigned) and `idivq` (signed) instructions are used. The dividend is stored in %rdx:%rax, the divisor is the operand, the quotient is stored in %rax, and the remainder in %rdx. The `cqto` instruction is used to sign-extend the value in %rax into %rdx:%rax before division.
example_explanation: This C code demonstrates 128-bit unsigned multiplication using inline assembly.  The `mulq` instruction multiplies the value in %rax (x) by the operand y. The result is a 128-bit value spread across %rax (lower 64 bits) and %rdx (upper 64 bits).  The assembly code moves the inputs, performs the multiplication, and then stores the result into the `result` variable (which has been defined to be 128 bits wide) demonstrating the use of the register pair to manage the extended precision of the calculation.
